plot_extraction.response_text:
In the isolated, perfectly ordered borough of Vondervotteimittiss, generations of inhabitants live identical lives centered on clocks, cabbages, routine, and the conviction that nothing worthwhile exists beyond their surrounding hills. Their greatest pride is the flawless town clock, whose strokes synchronize every timepiece and activity in the village.

Just before noon, a strange, sinister fiddler crosses the hills, dances erratically into town, and climbs the clock tower. He assaults the revered belfry-man, interferes with the clock, and causes it to strike thirteen. Every clock and watch in the borough follows suit, throwing meals, habits, animals, and inhabitants into chaos. As the intruder continues ringing the bell and playing his fiddle wildly from the tower, the narrator flees and calls upon supporters of accurate time and traditional order to return with him and drive the disruptive stranger out.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts the manner of a mock historical chronicle, presenting an absurd folktale with exaggerated scholarly seriousness. Its first-person narrator claims to be a scrupulous, impartial historian, invoking manuscripts, inscriptions, authorities, derivations, and archival evidence. This pose is deliberately undermined by the fanciful subject matter, comically unverifiable claims, and invented scholars and treatises. The result is sustained deadpan irony: the narrator’s formal confidence makes the borough’s irrational customs and impossible events appear all the more ridiculous.

The narrative voice is intrusive, theatrical, and openly conscious of its audience. It repeatedly addresses “the reader,” announces what will be explained later, comments on the adequacy of its own descriptions, and uses exclamations and rhetorical questions to direct emotional response. Although the narrator initially affects restraint and objectivity, his language grows increasingly partisan. The foreign intruder is called a “rascal,” “scoundrel,” “villain,” and “nincompoop,” while the conclusion becomes an explicit appeal to restore the old order. This shift exposes the supposed historian as emotionally aligned with the borough’s values and prejudices.

The diction combines ornate nineteenth-century prose with comic colloquialism. Elevated phrases such as “rigid impartiality,” “diligent collation of authorities,” and “remotest period of antiquity” sit beside homely references to cabbages, pigs, pipes, shoe buckles, and sauerkraut. Mock-scholarly Latin, pseudo-German names, bibliographical minutiae, French dance terms, and phonetic dialect all add to the linguistic density. The invented proper names are especially playful, relying on heavy consonants, reduplication, and grotesque sound patterns to suggest Dutch or German speech while functioning as verbal caricature.

Sentence structure is generally elaborate and cumulative. Long periodic sentences gather qualifications, parenthetical remarks, lists, and subordinate clauses before reaching their main point. Dashes are frequent and create comic pauses, abrupt corrections, emphatic afterthoughts, and changes of direction. Semicolons and colons support catalogues and formal exposition, while exclamation marks become more common as order collapses. Short sentences are reserved for emphatic reversals, especially the clock’s numbered strokes and the shocked response to “Thirteen!” The movement from expansive description to clipped call-and-response heightens the climactic disruption.

Repetition is the principal organising device. The borough consists of sixty identical houses; each garden has the same path, sundial, and twenty-four cabbages; each household contains nearly identical people, furnishings, foods, animals, and watches. Clocks and cabbages recur as visual motifs, civic emblems, and comic obsessions. Parallel phrasing reinforces the inhabitants’ mechanical conformity: they sit alike, dress alike, smoke alike, and repeat the clock’s strokes in unison. Even the council’s resolutions reduce civic philosophy to resistance to change, hostility toward the outside world, and devotion to “clocks and cabbages.” This patterned repetition gives the prose a clockwork rhythm while satirising social uniformity.

Description is highly visual, concrete, and grotesquely miniaturised. The setting resembles a toy village or animated clock: circular, enclosed, symmetrical, brightly coloured, and populated by tiny, round figures. Physical traits are exaggerated into caricature—large eyes, enormous chins, swollen stomachs, oversized buckles, and absurdly long coat-tails. Colour is used lavishly and incongruously, with orange clothing, green stockings, pink shoes, purple ribbons, red bricks, and black trim. Precise measurements and quantities lend counterfeit realism to an obviously artificial world.

The humour depends on escalation and incongruity. Minor details are treated as matters of immense civic importance, while genuine violence and supernatural disturbance are rendered as slapstick. The belfry-man’s beating becomes a percussion performance; animals with watches tied to their tails add to the chaos; clocks dance and pendulums writhe; overcooked cabbage and extinguished pipes are lamented as catastrophes. Lists lengthen as the disorder spreads, and polysyndeton—particularly strings of “and”—creates a breathless sense of accumulating noise and motion.

Dialogue is sparse until the climax, where it becomes rhythmic, communal, and phonetic. The numerical exchange between the great bell and the smaller watches resembles a ritual antiphony. Dialect spellings such as “von,” “doo,” “dvelf,” and “dirteen” produce broad comic characterisation and make the citizens sound as uniform in speech as they are in behaviour. Their simultaneous cries further erase individuality, turning the population into a chorus. Onomatopoeic and sound-oriented language—ticking, striking, puffing, scraping, squeaking, screeching, and caterwauling—makes the final scene acoustically crowded.

Structurally, the story proceeds from static order to explosive disorder. Most of the narrative patiently constructs the borough as an enclosed, changeless system. The stranger then crosses the forbidden hills shortly before noon, and the countdown creates temporal suspense. His irregular dancing, untimely music, and thirteenth bell stroke attack the community’s central principle: exact temporal coordination. The conclusion does not resolve the disturbance but converts the tale into a mock public appeal, preserving the narrator’s pseudo-documentary frame.

The dominant tone is whimsical, satirical, and burlesque, with an undercurrent of menace. The borough is picturesque but also narrow, complacent, xenophobic, and absurdly resistant to alteration. The intruder appears sinister, yet he also embodies spontaneity, asymmetry, music, and disorder in opposition to mechanical routine. The style therefore supports a satire of provincialism, unquestioned tradition, bureaucratic dignity, and obsessive regularity. Its distinctive effect comes from narrating cartoonish fantasy in the solemn language of scholarship, history, and civic emergency.

# The Thirteenth Stroke of Vondervotteimittiss

It has been asserted by persons of no learning whatever—and repeated, I regret to add, by Professor Knipperklatsch in the third appendix to his *Chronometrical Geography of the Lesser Hills*—that the borough of Vondervotteimittiss never existed. I shall not answer so transparent an absurdity. The brass seal now before me, bearing a cabbage rampant upon a clock-face proper, would alone confound such skepticism; and if further testimony were required, I might refer the reader to the worm-eaten municipal register of Bürgermeister Hans Puffenstumpf, to the inscription discovered beneath the eastern pig-trough, and to a memorandum in my own hand, written upon the very afternoon of the events herein related.

I claim only rigid impartiality. If, during the progress of this account, indignation should force from me such expressions as “rascal,” “scoundrel,” or “long-legged nincompoop,” the candid reader will attribute them not to prejudice, but to that moral accuracy without which history degenerates into mere fact.

Vondervotteimittiss lay, and perhaps still lies, in the exact middle of a circular valley enclosed by twelve smooth hills. Why twelve? Herr Doktor Doppelzinn maintains that each hill represented a month; Father Schnapps, in his *De Montibus Rotundis*, insists that the number arose from a shortage of hills; while the oldest inhabitants, whose authority is naturally superior because none of them could remember anything, declared that there had always been twelve and therefore could never be thirteen.

No road crossed those hills. No traveler descended them. No native climbed them, except once, in the reign of Bürgermeister Von Glump, when a boy named Peter Peepchen pursued a blue butterfly halfway up the southern slope. He was brought back by the Council, washed in vinegar, deprived of cabbage for two suppers, and compelled to apologize to the horizon.

Beyond the hills there was believed to be nothing worth mentioning. Certain controversialists allowed the possible existence of fog, wolves, foreigners, and bad time; but even these concessions were thought dangerously liberal.

The borough itself was a model of arrangement. It consisted of sixty houses—neither fifty-nine nor sixty-one—disposed in a perfect ring about a paved market-place. Each house was built of red brick, edged with black timber, roofed with blue slate, and furnished with a green door, three white windows, one brass knocker, and a chimney which leaned inward at precisely the same angle. Before each house stood a garden; through each garden ran a yellow path; beside each path rose a sundial; and around each sundial flourished twenty-four cabbages.

The number twenty-four has been disputed. I have counted them.

In the first garden were twenty-four cabbages; in the second, twenty-four; in the third, twenty-four; and so onward through the entire circumference, making, by the ordinary rules of multiplication, one thousand four hundred and forty cabbages. They were round cabbages, sound cabbages, glossy cabbages, and—until the fatal day—punctual cabbages. They opened their leaves at six in the morning, received water at seven, were inspected at eight, dusted at nine, praised at ten, and considered for dinner at eleven.

Every house contained a father, a mother, three children, a pig, a cat, a canary, two feather beds, six chairs, a cupboard, a copper kettle, and nine clocks. I except the Bürgermeister’s residence, which contained ten clocks, two pigs, and an official umbrella; but this was privilege, not irregularity.

The fathers were small, broad men, with round heads, round shoulders, round waistcoats, and stomachs of such civic magnificence that the buttons upon them seemed less fastenings than medals. They wore orange coats with tails reaching nearly to the ground, green stockings, pink shoes, and silver buckles large enough to serve, in an emergency, as dinner-plates. Their chins were prodigious. Their eyes were pale and prominent. Their hair was combed backward in seven ridges and tied with purple ribbon.

At sunrise each father wound his watch, opened his door, looked at his cabbages, looked at the sky, distrusted the sky, looked again at his watch, and said:

“Goot. It is morning.”

The mothers were equally regular, though somewhat wider. They wore scarlet petticoats, blue aprons, yellow caps, and wooden shoes painted with minute representations of clocks and cabbages. At six they stirred the porridge; at seven they polished the clocks; at eight they combed the children; at nine they combed the pig; at ten they cut cabbage; at eleven they put cabbage into the pot; and at twelve they served it, neither raw nor soft, but in that intermediate condition prescribed by Municipal Ordinance XLIV, paragraph C.

The children differed from their parents only in size and the absence of settled opinions concerning taxation. They marched three abreast to the schoolhouse, where Master Ticktack taught them the alphabet thus:

“A is for Alarm.  
B is for Bell.  
C is for Cabbage.  
D is for Dial.”

I suppress the remaining letters, partly because the reader can infer them and partly because Master Ticktack never discovered anything suitable for X.

As for the animals, they too were regulated. The cats slept from one until four, scratched from four until five, and watched the canaries from five until six. The canaries sang only on the quarter-hour. The pigs ate according to a printed table and were provided with little wooden watches tied to their tails, not because they could read the time, but because, as Councillor Grunzwig justly observed, “discipline begins vere understanding ends.”

All this order proceeded from the Great Clock.

The Great Clock occupied the tower in the centre of the market-place. The tower was one hundred and one feet high according to the town survey, ninety-eight according to its shadow, and seven hundred according to the guidebook; but as the guidebook included moral elevation, the discrepancy is easily reconciled. Its walls were white, its roof was crimson, and upon its summit revolved a gilded weathercock shaped like a cabbage with wings.

The clock-face was enormous and blue. Its figures were gold; its hands were black; its two eyes—if I may employ a metaphor sanctioned by Archivist Blinkenbrood—looked down upon the borough with an expression of grave disapproval. The pendulum, visible through a glass panel, swung with a majestic clack—right, left; right, left—like the legs of some enormous brass magistrate pacing forever between two opinions.

At every hour the Great Clock struck. At every stroke the nine clocks in every house replied; the fathers repeated the number; the mothers nodded; the children counted upon their fingers; the canaries chirped; the pigs wagged their watches; and the cabbages, according to a manuscript too delicate for public handling, inclined their outer leaves.

The care of this noble instrument belonged to the hereditary Belfry-Man, old Dietrich Dunderkopf, the seventeenth of his line. He lived in a room immediately beneath the bell, ate by the pendulum, slept by the escapement, and had not descended the tower in forty-two years. His beard was twisted into two cords to prevent its entanglement in the wheels. His left eye magnified and his right eye diminished, from long use of lenses; thus, when he looked at a man, he saw him simultaneously as a giant and a beetle, which must have been invaluable in forming impartial judgments.

Every day at eleven minutes before noon, Dunderkopf oiled the fourth wheel. At nine minutes before noon, he tested the hammer. At seven minutes before noon, he looked from the northern window. At five minutes before noon, he looked from the southern window. At three minutes before noon, he took off his cap. At one minute before noon, he placed his hand upon his heart.

Then came twelve.

Then came dinner.

Then came contentment.

Such had been the custom from the remotest antiquity—from a period, indeed, before which no records survive because, as the Council wisely resolved, nothing had yet happened.

The fundamental statutes of Vondervotteimittiss were three:

First: That whatever had been was preferable to whatever might be.

Second: That whatever lay beyond the hills was either impossible or improper.

Third: That no respectable man required more than clocks and cabbages.

These principles produced happiness of the most complete and motionless description. No citizen was richer than his neighbor by more than two spoons. No house was painted differently. No song possessed an unexpected note. No child asked “Why?” twice. Even dreams were reported each morning to the Clerk of Slumbers and corrected when eccentric.

Yet upon the twenty-seventh day of Sauerkraut, in the year 18—, there occurred an event which I tremble to record. I was present. I saw it. I heard it. I have, furthermore, a dent in my hat caused by a descending turnip, though turnips, I admit, are not otherwise material to the narrative.

The morning began with perfect propriety. At six, the doors opened. At seven, the cabbages were watered. At eight, the pigs were combed. At nine, the Council met to debate whether the western sundials cast shadows excessively to the east. At ten, the debate was adjourned, all parties having agreed that the sun was probably at fault. At eleven, six hundred cooking-pots received six hundred cabbages.

At thirteen minutes before noon, however, little Greta Glumple—whose testimony must be treated cautiously, since she was only eight and had once imagined a cloud—pointed toward the eastern hill.

Something stood upon its summit.

The fathers lifted their spectacles. The mothers shaded their eyes. The children opened their mouths. The pigs, being lower, saw nothing.

At first the object resembled a black pin stuck into the sky. Then it lengthened. Then it bent. Then it sprang upward, flourished two arms, kicked one leg toward the clouds, and began descending the hill in a manner so contrary to gravity, dignity, and municipal precedent that several citizens sat down without consulting their watches.

It was a man.

Or, to be exact, it was a thing dressed as a man, though no proper man could have arranged himself so maliciously. He was excessively tall and outrageously thin. His coat was half black and half yellow, with one tail short and the other dragging behind him like a disappointed serpent. One stocking was red, the other striped. His shoes turned up at the toes and bore tiny bells which jingled at all the wrong moments. Upon his head perched a sugarloaf hat decorated with a white feather, a brass spoon, and what appeared to be the wing of a bat.

His face was narrow; his nose was long; his chin was longer. His eyes glittered beneath shaggy brows, and his mouth stretched from cheek to cheek in a grin of insufferable arithmetic—as though he had counted us and found one too many.

Under his arm he carried a fiddle.

Now, the fiddle is not unknown to historical science. I have inspected three. But this instrument was of a crooked, reddish wood, with strings that seemed to twitch before they were touched, and a bow so long that the rascal used it alternately as cane, balancing-pole, sword, fishing-rod, and instrument of personal insult.

Down the hill he came—hop, slide, twirl, tumble, recover; hop, slide, twirl, tumble, recover—playing all the while a tune which began nowhere, proceeded backward, and ended before it began. It was not a march, for it marched sideways; not a waltz, for it had five feet; not a gavotte, though Madame Trippentrapp detected in it a corrupted *pas de chou*; and certainly not music, unless cats falling through crockery may be admitted to the conservatory.

At nine minutes before noon he entered the eastern gate.

“Stop!” cried the gatekeeper.

The stranger leaped over him.

“Name!” cried the registrar.

The stranger played three squeaks and a groan.

“Business!” cried the tax collector.

The stranger bowed, removed the collector’s hat with his bow, placed it upon a pig, and danced onward.

O villain! O unlicensed caterwauler! Yet I proceed calmly.

Through the market-place he zigzagged, though all civic movement had always been circular. He skipped across gardens, crushed exactly one cabbage in each, turned the sundials backward, opened doors that should have been shut, shut doors that should have been open, wound the tails of seventeen cats, and exchanged the watches of Councillors Knopf and Knapp, who immediately accused each other of being three minutes old.

The fathers shouted. The mothers shrieked. The children applauded until corrected. The canaries sang between quarter-hours. The pigs pursued the tax collector’s hat.

At six minutes before noon the stranger reached the clock tower.

The door was locked by seven bolts, three chains, and an ordinance. He touched it with the tip of his bow.

It flew open.

He entered. We heard his shoes upon the stair:

Jingle—scrape—jingle—thump!

Round and round he climbed, while above us old Dunderkopf, having completed his inspection of the southern window, prepared himself in innocence for the sacred stroke.

At four minutes before noon came a crash.

At three minutes, a yell.

At two minutes, the belfry window burst outward, and Dunderkopf’s cap floated down.

At one minute, we saw them.

There, behind the great blue face, struggled the hereditary guardian and the fiddling scoundrel. Dunderkopf wielded his oil-can; the stranger parried with his bow. Dunderkopf thrust with a winding-key; the stranger ducked, spun, and struck the old man’s bald crown—ping!—then his left shoulder—pong!—then his right knee—piddle-paddle-ping! In this infamous manner he converted the assault into a species of percussion accompaniment, while his fiddle squealed above it like a fox disputing theology.

The citizens stood frozen. No one had ever been beaten in the belfry. There was no regulation for it.

Then the clock began to strike.

BONG!

“Von!” cried every father.

Ting! went every household clock.

BONG!

“Doo!” cried every mother.

Ting! ting! replied the watches.

BONG!

“Dree!” shouted the children.

BONG!

“Four!”

The stranger appeared at the highest window. He had tied poor Dunderkopf to the pendulum by his beard. With every swing the old man traveled right and left, right and left, his boots describing arcs of melancholy precision.

BONG!

“Five!”

The cabbage-pots bubbled.

BONG!

“Six!”

The fathers drew their chairs toward the tables.

BONG!

“Seven!”

The mothers lifted their ladles.

BONG!

“Eight!”

The children tucked napkins beneath their chins.

BONG!

“Nine!”

The cats approached the scraps.

BONG!

“Ten!”

The canaries ceased singing.

BONG!

“Eleven!”

Every knife rose.

BONG!

“Dvelf!”

Every knife descended. Every lid came off. Every mouth opened. Every citizen inhaled the lawful perfume of cabbage.

There should have been silence.

There was a pause—small, black, and dreadful.

The stranger grinned.

He seized the hammer-rope with both hands, kicked his heels above his head, and dropped.

BONG!

“DIRTEEN!”

The word did not at first seem to belong to any human language. It burst simultaneously from six hundred citizens, sixty pigs, an uncertain number of children who counted twice, and old Dunderkopf, who uttered it upside down while passing the left extremity of the pendulum.

Thirteen!

Reader, imagine it if you can. I cannot, and I was there.

Every clock in Vondervotteimittiss, from the Bürgermeister’s ten-foot regulator to the baby’s tin repeater, struck again. Mantel clocks hopped from mantelpieces. Cuckoos rushed from their doors and refused to return. Pendulums twisted like snakes. Minute-hands chased hour-hands. Alarms exploded without appointments. Watches tore loose from waistcoat pockets and spun upon their chains; and the wooden watches attached to the pigs’ tails clattered so violently that the pigs, supposing themselves pursued by carpenters, galloped through the market-place.

Dinner collapsed.

Some cabbages, interpreting the extra stroke as an instruction to boil another hour, dissolved at once into green vapor. Others hardened like cannonballs. One leaped from its pot, bounded through a window, and struck my hat—the dent to which I have already alluded. Soup ran uphill. Spoons rang against foreheads. The fathers swallowed their pipes; the mothers put tobacco into the sugar bowls; the children, released from arithmetic by the failure of twelve, began counting everything beyond necessity.

“Dirteen, fourteen, fifteen—”

“Silence!” roared Master Ticktack. “Dere is no fifteen after dinner!”

But the disorder increased.

The cats barked at the canaries. The canaries crowed. The pigs climbed garden walls. The sundials cast shadows in several directions, although the sun, to its credit, remained comparatively sober. Councillor Knopf discovered that Councillor Knapp’s watch made him younger and refused to return it. Madame Trippentrapp danced a funeral polka. The tax collector chased his hat, which still rode the largest pig and appeared to have assumed executive authority.

Above all sounded that diabolical fiddle.

The intruder sat astride the weathercock, sawing and scraping, jingling and screeching, while with one foot he pulled the bell-rope and with the other he kicked the minute-hand backward. The tune multiplied itself. It came from chimneys, kettles, keyholes, cupboard hinges, shoe buckles, and the hollow interiors of cabbages. The tower swayed. The houses nodded. The sixty green doors opened and shut in rhythm. The blue roofs lifted like hats. Even the twelve hills seemed to bob, though Professor Knipperklatsch later attributed this to collective dizziness.

“Stop him!” cried the Bürgermeister.

“How?” cried the Council.

“By precedent!”

“There is none!”

“Then appoint a committee!”

A committee was appointed, but before its chairman could state the purpose of its formation, the Great Clock struck fourteen.

Or perhaps it struck one again. Authorities differ, and my ink was shaken from the bottle.

At that instant every routine in the borough became entangled with every other. Citizens went to bed while chewing dinner, rose before lying down, wound their pigs, watered their watches, polished their children, scolded their cabbages, and placed their clocks in the oven. Three fathers departed for school. Nine canaries were elected to the Council. The Clerk of Slumbers recorded an awake dream and fined himself.

I confess—and history shall not blush for prudent retreat—that I fled.

I passed the eastern gate while the villain’s laughter rattled the windows behind me. I crossed the forbidden slope. I reached the summit and looked back once.

There lay Vondervotteimittiss, no longer circular but wriggling; its roofs seesawing, its chimneys puffing backward, its inhabitants running clockwise and counterclockwise at once. Over the tower flapped the bat-wing feather of the fiddler’s hat. Beneath him swung poor Dunderkopf. Around him spun the hands of the Great Clock.

And again the bell sounded.

BONG!

How many strokes have followed, I do not know. Perhaps it is striking still.

Therefore I make this appeal—not as partisan, not as citizen, not as a man whose luncheon was ruined, but as an impartial historian devoted solely to truth, order, punctual digestion, and the ancient liberties of cabbage.

Let every friend of accurate time come forward! Let all who wind their watches on Sunday, who respect the hour, who distrust irregular music, who believe that twelve is sufficient for any clock and that hills were intended to keep strangers out—let them take up broom, umbrella, warming-pan, cabbage-knife, or other constitutional weapon!

We shall return to Vondervotteimittiss.

We shall climb the tower.

We shall rescue Dunderkopf, restore the pendulum, boil the cabbages anew, return the tax collector’s hat, and drive that scraping, jingling, grinning, thirteenth-stroking rascal beyond the twelve respectable hills.

Who is with me?

free_generation.response_text:
The Bell at Low Tide

Every morning, just before sunrise, Mara Venn walked down to the harbor and listened for the bell beneath the sea.

Most people in Bellwether called it a legend. The old fishermen did not. They would pause when the tide was lowest, remove their caps, and turn toward the eastern reef. Sometimes there was only the click of pebbles rolling in the undertow. Sometimes there was a sound like iron striking iron, distant and solemn.

One note.

Then silence.

Mara had heard it seventeen times.

Her father had heard it once, on the morning he disappeared.

He had been Bellwether’s lighthouse keeper, though the lighthouse no longer required keeping. Its electric lamp switched itself on at dusk and off at dawn. A brass mechanism rotated the lens with a steady hum, and once a month a technician came from the mainland to inspect the gears. Even so, Tomas Venn had climbed the spiral stairs every evening, polished the windows, checked the emergency oil, and written the weather into a leather-bound logbook.

“A machine can make light,” he used to say. “That doesn’t mean it knows who needs it.”

After his disappearance, Mara took over the ritual.

She was nineteen then. By the time she heard the bell for the seventeenth time, she was twenty-seven, and the lighthouse had been scheduled for demolition.

The letter arrived on a Tuesday in October.

UNSAFE STRUCTURE, it declared. EXCESSIVE COASTAL EROSION. REPLACEMENT BEACON APPROVED.

At the bottom, beneath a cluster of official stamps, someone had added a handwritten note:

Demolition begins Monday. Please remove personal effects.

Mara read the letter twice in the lighthouse kitchen. Rain ticked against the windows. On the stove, the kettle began to whistle.

She folded the paper, placed it under her father’s blue cup, and climbed to the lantern room.

Beyond the glass, the sea was the color of hammered lead. Waves broke against the eastern reef, where the drowned bell waited under thirty feet of water.

According to the legend, there had once been a town beyond the reef. Not a grand town, but a collection of stone houses, a chapel, two inns, and a market square. Its name had been Orison. During the winter of 1811, a storm had struck the coast for nine days. The cliffs collapsed, the sea flooded the valley, and Orison vanished before dawn.

Only the chapel bell survived.

It rang at low tide, people said, whenever someone at sea had lost the way home.

Mara had never believed that part. Her father had known the sea better than anyone. He could name winds by scent and judge the hour by the angle of gulls. He had not been lost.

He had chosen to leave.

At least, that was what she had told herself.

On Sunday night, the storm came.

It was not violent at first. The rain arrived in thin silver lines, and the sea withdrew farther than Mara had ever seen it go. Black rocks rose from the water like the backs of sleeping animals. Tangled ropes of weed shone beneath the lighthouse beam.

Mara stood in the lantern room with her father’s final logbook open in her hands.

She had read the last entry hundreds of times.

November 3. Wind east-northeast. Barometer falling. Heard bell at 05:14. Light visible beyond reef. Going to investigate.

There was no mention of a boat, yet one had vanished from the harbor that morning: a small green skiff belonging to the lighthouse. Three days later, an oar washed ashore. Nothing else was found.

Mara closed the book.

Far below, someone knocked on the lighthouse door.

She descended with a lamp in one hand. When she opened the door, she found Elias Rook leaning into the wind.

He had been her closest friend when they were children and might have become something more if Mara had not made a habit of holding the world at arm’s length. Now he repaired boats at the harbor and lived above his workshop with a yellow dog named Thimble.

“The demolition crew crossed on the last ferry,” he said. Rain ran from his dark hair. “They’ll start at seven.”

“I know.”

“I thought you might need help packing.”

“I’ve packed.”

He glanced past her. The kitchen shelves were full. Her father’s coat still hung beside the stove. Charts remained pinned to the walls.

“Mara.”

“I said I’ve packed.”

Thunder murmured beyond the horizon.

Elias stepped inside and shut the door. “They’re staying at the Crown. Half of them are drunk, and the other half wish they were. If the storm worsens, they’ll postpone.”

“It won’t matter.”

“What won’t?”

“The lighthouse. Whether they destroy it tomorrow or next week, it will still be gone.”

Elias studied her face. “Come live in town.”

“I have a house in town.”

“You have four rooms filled with dust and unopened letters.”

“They’re my letters.”

“And your dust.”

She almost smiled.

Then the bell rang.

The sound came through the walls, low and enormous.

Mara’s lamp trembled in her hand.

Elias turned toward the sea.

A second note rolled across the exposed reef.

Mara had never heard it ring twice.

She pulled open the door. The rain had stopped. Clouds boiled above the horizon, but directly over the eastern reef the sky was clear, revealing a cold spread of stars.

The sea continued to retreat.

Channels appeared between the rocks. Stone walls emerged, dripping and weed-covered. A narrow road revealed itself beneath the water, running from the shore toward the reef.

At its far end, a light moved.

Not the white beam of a modern lamp, but a warm, golden flame.

Elias whispered, “What is that?”

Mara was already reaching for her coat.

He caught her wrist. “No.”

“My father saw a light.”

“Eight years ago.”

“He saw it after the bell rang.”

“And then he vanished.”

She pulled free. “Exactly.”

The path across the reef was slick but unmistakable. Flat stones lay fitted together beneath barnacles and sand. On either side, water streamed through the ruins of walls. Fish flashed in moonlit pools. Crabs crawled across thresholds that had not known footsteps for two centuries.

Elias followed, carrying a coil of rope and two lanterns.

“You should go back,” Mara told him.

“So should you.”

The golden light drifted ahead, sometimes disappearing behind the broken remains of houses. No one held it. It floated at shoulder height, steady despite the wind.

They passed a stone arch with letters carved into it. Most were worn away, but Mara traced the remaining shapes.

ORIS—

The drowned town.

Far behind them, the lighthouse beam swept over Bellwether. For a moment its pale light crossed the ruins, and Mara saw chimneys, a dry fountain, and the roofless chapel rising from the reef.

Then darkness returned.

The road descended.

Water covered Mara’s boots, then reached her knees. The tide should have been turning, but the sea continued to drain away, flowing east as if the moon had cracked and all the oceans were spilling into the sky.

At the chapel door, the golden light stopped.

Above them, in a roofless tower, hung the bell.

It was smaller than Mara had imagined, green with age, tangled in weed. No rope descended from it.

Still, it moved.

The bell sounded a third time.

The stones beneath Mara’s feet shuddered.

Inside the chapel, where an altar had once stood, a spiral staircase turned downward into darkness.

Elias lifted his lantern. “That was never in the stories.”

“My father didn’t know the stories were true.”

“Mara, listen to me. The tide will come back.”

She looked at the staircase. “Then wait here.”

“No.”

“You can’t stop me.”

“I know.” He tied one end of the rope around a pillar. “That’s the problem.”

They descended.

The staircase seemed much deeper than the reef allowed. Fifty steps passed, then a hundred. The air grew warmer. The walls were dry and marked with lines of writing.

Mara held her lantern close.

Names covered every stone.

Ada Lorne, 1843.

Jon Bell, 1907.

Peter and Samuel Marr, 1926.

Some had dates. Some had only initials. Others were accompanied by short messages.

Forgive me.

Tell her I tried.

The fog came too quickly.

Mara found her father’s name near the bottom.

Tomas Venn, 2016.

Beneath it, in his narrow handwriting:

Mara, do not follow the light.

She stopped.

Elias read the words over her shoulder.

For eight years, Mara had imagined what she would say if she ever found proof that her father had not drowned. She had rehearsed accusations, pleas, and questions. She had dreamed of striking him. She had dreamed of embracing him.

She had never imagined a warning.

From below came the scrape of wood.

The stair ended at a beach beneath a starless sky.

A black sea stretched before them. Along the shore rested dozens of boats: rowboats, fishing vessels, canoes, a steam launch with a broken funnel, even the splintered hull of something like a Viking ship. Their styles belonged to different centuries, but none showed signs of decay.

At the edge of the water stood a man in a gray coat.

He was bent over a green skiff, pushing it toward the sea.

“Father?”

The man froze.

He turned slowly.

Tomas Venn looked exactly as he had on the morning he vanished. His beard was touched with frost. A fresh cut crossed his cheek. His eyes widened when he saw Mara.

“No,” he said.

The word was not wonder. It was grief.

Mara ran to him anyway.

She struck his chest with both hands.

“You left me!”

He stumbled but did not defend himself.

“You left me alone. You didn’t write. You didn’t come back. I waited every day, and you—”

Her voice broke.

He wrapped his arms around her.

For a moment she resisted. Then she pressed her face against his coat and smelled lamp oil, salt, and the soap he had always used.

“I’m sorry,” he whispered. “I’m so sorry.”

Elias stood apart, his lantern lowered.

Tomas looked over Mara’s shoulder. “Who is that?”

“Elias Rook.”

“Little Elias?”

“Not so little anymore,” Elias said.

Tomas looked from one to the other, bewildered. “How long?”

“Eight years.”

He released Mara. “For me, it has been less than an hour.”

The black water made no sound. Far out at sea, hundreds of golden lights wandered across the darkness.

“What is this place?” Mara asked.

“I don’t know. A harbor between harbors, perhaps.” He touched the green skiff. “When I heard the bell, I saw a light beyond the reef. I followed it. There was a boat caught in the fog—a family, three children. Their lantern had gone out. I guided them here.”

“Where are they?”

“They took another boat. They said it would carry them home.”

“And you?”

“My skiff was damaged. I’ve been repairing it.”

“For eight years?”

“For an hour.”

A sound like distant thunder rolled across the beach.

The boats shifted on the sand.

Elias looked up the stair. Water trickled over the lowest step.

“The tide is coming back,” he said.

Tomas pushed the skiff harder. “Then you must go.”

“We all must go,” Mara said.

“I can’t.”

“Why?”

He pointed to the black sea. One of the wandering lights had separated from the others. It moved toward shore, revealing a small boat.

Inside sat a woman and a child.

The woman rowed with one oar. The child lay motionless in her lap.

“They’re lost,” Tomas said. “That is what the bell means. Someone must bring them to the staircase.”

“Then bring them,” Mara said. “We’ll wait.”

“The way opens only at low tide. If you wait, you’ll remain here until it opens again.”

“Eight years from now?”

“Or eighty. Or eight minutes. Time has no tide in this place.”

Water poured down the stairs, covering the first two steps.

Elias seized Mara’s hand. “We have to go.”

She stared at her father. “Come with us.”

Tomas looked toward the woman and child. Their boat had begun to turn in a slow circle.

“If I leave, they may never find shore.”

“Someone else can guide them.”

“There is no one else.”

“There’s always someone else! That’s what you taught yourself so you could keep choosing strangers over me.”

He flinched.

The truth of it hung between them, sharper than anger.

All her childhood, Tomas had answered bells. Wrecks, fires, storms, missing sailors—he had gone wherever light was needed. Bellwether called him brave. Mara had called him Father, but rarely in his presence.

He took off his gray coat and placed it around her shoulders.

“You’re right,” he said. “I believed being needed was the same as being good. Sometimes it was easier to save strangers. Strangers never asked me to stay.”

The water reached Elias’s ankles.

Mara wanted to hate him. Hatred would have been solid ground. Instead, she saw him as he was: loving and flawed, brave and afraid, standing beside a patched boat under an empty sky.

She gripped the coat at her throat.

“Will I see you again?”

Tomas looked at the golden lights.

“Yes,” he said, and then, because he had always lied badly, “I don’t know.”

The woman’s boat drifted farther from shore.

Tomas pushed the skiff into the water.

Elias started up the stairs, pulling the rope hand over hand. Mara followed as far as the first step, then turned.

Her father had climbed into the skiff. He raised one hand.

She raised hers.

“I heard the bell seventeen times,” she called.

He smiled. “I rang it eighteen.”

Then the darkness took him.

The staircase flooded quickly.

Mara and Elias climbed as water swirled around their knees, their waists, their chests. Elias went first, hauling on the rope. Mara followed, fighting the weight of her father’s coat.

Halfway up, one of the lanterns went out.

Near the top, the rope jerked loose.

They stumbled into the chapel as a wave crashed through the doorway.

The drowned town had vanished beneath churning water. Only the chapel tower remained above the sea. The path to shore was gone.

Elias tied the rope around Mara’s waist.

“What are you doing?”

“You’re the better swimmer.”

“That makes no sense.”

“I know. I’m terrified.”

The honesty of it startled a laugh from her.

Another wave broke over the chapel wall.

Together, they jumped.

The sea was winter-cold. It dragged Mara downward, filling her ears with thunder. Her father’s coat billowed around her like wings. For one mad instant, she thought she saw golden lights below—streets, windows, people walking through Orison as it had been before the storm.

Then Elias pulled the rope, and she kicked toward the surface.

The lighthouse beam found them.

White light crossed the waves and returned, crossed and returned, each time showing the direction of shore.

A machine can make light, Mara thought. That doesn’t mean it knows who needs it.

But perhaps a machine did not need to know. Perhaps someone only had to look.

They reached the rocks near dawn.

The demolition crew found them on the lighthouse steps, wrapped in blankets, bruised and shivering. Their foreman stared at the flooded causeway and declared them the two greatest fools on the coast.

Then he noticed the crack in the lighthouse.

It ran from the foundation to the lantern room.

“Storm did that,” he said.

“Can you repair it?” Mara asked.

He shook his head. “Not safely.”

At nine o’clock, the eastern wall collapsed.

At eleven, the tower followed.

The lantern room fell last, turning once in the pale morning before breaking against the rocks. Glass scattered like ice. The great lens split cleanly in two.

Mara watched without crying.

By spring, a steel beacon stood at the end of the harbor wall. It was short, ugly, and reliable. Sailors complained that its light lacked character, but they trusted it in fog.

Mara moved into her house in town.

She opened the letters. She swept the dust. Elias built shelves in the front room, and Thimble slept beneath the window. Neither Mara nor Elias spoke about forever. They began with breakfast, then supper, then the next morning.

The salvage company recovered the lighthouse bell from the ruins. It was not the bell of Orison, only a small brass bell that had once hung in the kitchen.

Mara mounted it above her door.

Years passed.

On nights when storms covered the sea, lost boats still appeared in the harbor, guided by a light no chart recorded. Their crews told strange stories: of a green skiff, a gray-coated man, and a lantern burning gold against the fog.

Mara listened but never interrupted.

Then, one autumn morning, when the tide was lower than anyone remembered, the bell beneath the sea rang.

Mara was no longer young. Silver threaded her hair. Elias stood beside her on the shore, his hand warm in hers.

The bell sounded once.

Twice.

Seventeen times.

At the eighteenth note, a golden light appeared beyond the reef.

Mara closed her eyes.

She could have followed it. Part of her always would.

Instead, she lifted the kitchen bell from the basket at her feet. She had brought it every low tide for forty years, though she had never admitted why.

She rang it once in answer.

Across the water, the golden light paused.

Then it turned east, toward the brightening horizon, and slowly disappeared.

Mara stood listening until the sea covered the road to Orison.

When at last she and Elias walked home, the sun rose behind them, and every window in Bellwether caught the light.
